transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-24 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Vargas (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Evergreen Head of ML Ops), Jonah Blake (Evergreen Platform Eng), Sara Thompson (Evergreen Procurement)

Summary:
Quick renewal check-in focused on Evergreen's upcoming Jan renewal window, proposed capacity uplift (dedicated pool + burst), and scope for adding EU private region with an onprem-like VPC pilot. Customer asked clarifying questions on failover, KMS, and pricing for burst usage. Agreed next steps for pricing, benchmarks, and legal redlines.

Topics covered:
- Renewal timing and target start of new term (2028-01-15)
- Capacity uplift: committed GPUs vs burst credits
- Multi-region: EU private pilot and APAC future interest
- Security baseline: SOC2 scope, KMS/HSM, audit logs
- Performance expectations: p50/p95 latency targets and continuous batching impact
- Contract mechanics: SOW, billing cadence, termination / rollback clauses

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Short agenda from our side — renewal timing, capacity numbers, and then Diego will walk through the EU private pilot brief.
[00:18] Priya: Thanks, Maya. We wanted to make sure we're aligned on numbers so procurement can finalize. Our renewal is up mid-Jan so we need to decide on committed capacity by end of December.
[00:30] Maya: Got it. Current proposal we sent last week was 120k token-hours committed / month, with a burst bucket on top. That was one of the options - do you want me to re-share?
[00:42] Jonah: Quick question — that 120k, is that equivalent to the ~12 concurrent workers we run today or is it more throughput? Our traffic is spiky end of month.
[00:55] Diego: Good question. The commit maps to throughput depending on model and sequence length. For your 40-token avg sequences on the 7B family we profiled ~11–13 concurrent generator slots. The burst is intended to cover those end-of-month spikes.
[01:12] Priya: And the burst pricing — is that pay-as-you-go at a premium or is it discounted if we pre-buy? Sara, what's preferred?
[01:20] Sara: Procurement likes predictability. If there's an option to carve a small reserved burst bucket with a lower unit price we prefer that.
[01:28] Maya: We can offer a tiered burst add-on. Option A: pure PAYG burst at 1.6x unit price. Option B: pre-purchase burst credits at 1.2x but with a 6-month min. We'll put both in the spreadsheet.
[01:40] Jonah: Nice. On the EU private pilot — can Diego talk about networking and KMS? We need to know if we can bring our own HSM or if Redwood uses a managed KMS.
[01:50] Diego: Sure. For the pilot we recommend Redwood Private in a customer VPC. We support KMS integrations — you can bring keys. For HSM there are a couple of deployment patterns: 1) customer-hosted HSM proxied into the control plane, or 2) partner HSM in-region. There are tradeoffs in latency for the envelope unwrap call, but we've done both.
[02:10] Priya: That latency call — is it in the critical path for every token? We need to ensure it won't blow up p95.
[02:18] Diego: No, the KMS unwrap is only during model load / session start. It isn't per-token. The per-token cost is dominated by GPU compute and KV cache access.
[02:28] Priya: Gotcha. Ok that's a relief.
[02:33] Maya: Diego, do you mind sharing the EU benchmark summary you ran with the 7B quantized variant? Evergreen's profile was in that runbook, right?
[02:40] Diego: Yep, I'll attach the CSV. Quick summary: in eu-west-1 with our quantized variant we saw p50 ~45ms and p95 ~210ms for your 40-token median requests at 400 RPS burst. For dedicated pools we can get p95 down to ~150ms when we reserve higher concurrency and enable continuous batching tuning.
[03:00] Jonah: 400 RPS burst — that's higher than our current peaks but matches what we expect after next quarter product rollout. How does Redwood handle fallback if dedicated capacity is saturated?
[03:12] Maya: We have smart routing policies. We can: 1) route overflow to a compatible hosted model variant, 2) throttle/queue requests, or 3) failover to pre-warmed burst nodes depending on the policy you choose. For Evergreen we suggested a mixed policy — route non-critical traf to hosted, keep critical low-latency traffic for dedicated.
[03:30] Priya: On the SLA side, if we route to hosted during overflow does that affect our SLA uptime?
[03:38] Maya: Good point — routed overflow will be outside the dedicated SLA but we can define a contractual fallback SLA. We'll call it out in the SOW with explicit metrics and fallback notice windows.
[03:48] Sara: On billing cadence — can we do monthly invoicing with true-up or do you prefer quarterly? Our finance team prefers monthly for cashflow.
[03:56] Maya: Monthly with a monthly true-up is doable. We might need slightly different invoicing items for committed vs burst credits but we'll accommodate monthly.
[04:05] Jonah: Diego, you mentioned caching — can you explain the KV caching impact again? We sometimes see latency cliffs on long conversations.
[04:14] Diego: Sure. Our KV cache keeps previous tokens in GPU memory for cached sessions. If session context is long and misses the cache, we evict and re-warm which can spike latency. For Evergreen's workload we recommended a larger per-session KV cache and sticky routing by user to reduce cache misses — that will help smooth p95.
[04:33] Priya: Are there extra costs for higher KV allocation?
[04:36] Diego: Not a separate line item typically; it's baked into the instance sizing. If you ask for unusually high per-session allocations we may recommend larger instance types which affects unit cost. We'll show a delta in the pricing sheet.
[04:48] Priya: Security check — SOC2 and audit logs: we need proof that access to logs and model artifacts is locked down and retention policy supports 90 days in-region.
[05:00] Maya: We are SOC2 Type II compliant and we'll include the SOC report. Audit logs can be streamed to your SIEM and retained per your policy in-region for 90+ days. For EU private we can assure in-region retention.
[05:14] Sara: We also need data residency language in the contract around not moving logs out of EU without consent.
[05:20] Maya: Noted — we'll propose explicit residency clauses and an escalation process.
[05:25] Priya: One last technical — for the private pilot, what's the expected lead time to provision an EU cluster with KMS integration? We're aiming for Jan pilot start.
[05:35] Diego: If we get network peering and KMS access in the next two weeks, typical lead time is 3–4 weeks for provision + validation. So it's tight but doable for a mid-Jan pilot if legal and procurement move quickly.
[05:47] Jonah: We'll try to prioritize the network info. I'll send the traffic profile and our internal SLOs.
[05:52] Maya: Great. Recap: Redwood will send updated pricing with burst options, Diego will send benchmark CSV and runbook, Evergreen to share traffic profile and Sara will send contract redlines. We'll follow up with a provisioning calendar.
[05:58] Priya: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[06:00] Maya: Thanks all — we'll circle up next week if there are outstanding items.

Notes about transcription accuracy: Speaker labels sometimes merged and a couple technical terms transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV cache" was at one point transcribed as "K V cash") — refer to attached runbook and CSVs for authoritative numbers.

Attachments referenced: tiered_pricing_evergreen_v2.xlsx (link sent in chat), eu_private_benchmark_2027-11-20.csv, redwood_sla_and_residency_draft.pdf

End of transcript.
